197.title: The universal form (11.9–11.31)
197.hook: Arjuna gets what he asked for, and it's brighter than a thousand suns
197.howItsDone: The vishvarupa, the universal form of Gita chapter eleven, is painted, sculpted and staged across Hindu art and temple traditions, and many devotees read the chapter with awe as the Gita's great vision.

segments.voice: Yesterday, divyam chakshuh: Arjuna asked to see, and got a divine eye. Your line was show me. Today, he's shown.

One sun at noon is already too bright to look at. Add a second beside it. Then ten. Then a hundred. Then a thousand, all at once, all blazing. You can't look at it. You can't look away. That's the measure the Gita reaches for when Arjuna, with his new divine eye, finally sees what he asked to see. Sanjaya, telling it, has no ordinary comparison left, so he stacks up suns.
screen: `ONE SUN AT NOON.` → `THEN A THOUSAND, AT ONCE.` → `TOO BRIGHT TO LOOK AT.`

segments.voice: Sanjaya tells it. Having spoken, the great lord of yoga showed Arjuna his supreme form. Many mouths and eyes, many wonders, divine ornaments, divine weapons raised. Faces turned in every direction. Verse twelve: if the light of a thousand suns were to blaze up in the sky all at once, it might be like the splendor of that great being. Verse thirteen: there, in the body of the god of gods, Arjuna saw the whole universe, divided in countless ways, gathered as one. His hair stands on end. He bows his head, joins his palms, and speaks. At first it's wonder. I see all the gods in your body, and all kinds of beings. Brahma on his lotus, the sages, the divine serpents. I see you everywhere, with countless arms and eyes. No end, no middle, no beginning. The sun and moon are your eyes. Then it turns. The mouths have fangs. The worlds are trembling, and so am I. Arjuna sees the warriors of both armies, the men he's about to fight, his own teachers and great-uncle among them, rushing into those mouths like rivers running into the ocean, like moths flying into a flame. Some are caught between the teeth. It's beautiful and it's terrifying, and the Gita doesn't soften either. Verse thirty-one: tell me, who are you, in this fierce form? I bow to you. Be gracious. I want to understand you; I don't know what you're doing. That's the universal form: everything, seen at once, including the parts that frighten us.

segments.voice: Feel your own body breathing, then widen: the room, the street, the city, the whole country at this hour, people waking and sleeping, being born and dying, then the earth turning in sunlight. Let it be too big to hold, and notice what that feels like: wonder, fear, or both. Then come back to one breath.
Vishvarupa. The universal form: the whole universe seen at once in God's body, brighter than a thousand suns, wonderful and terrible.
Your line: a thousand suns. Arjuna asked to see, and he saw. See you tomorrow.

198.title: "I am Time" (11.32–11.34)
198.hook: the line Oppenheimer remembered, and what the Sanskrit word actually says
198.howItsDone: Hindus read Gita 11.32–34 in different ways: some as a warrior's duty and the power of time over every life, others, following Gandhi, as an allegory of the inner battle; the image of Kala, time, also appears in the worship of Shiva and Kali.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vishvarupa: the universal form, brighter than a thousand suns, and Arjuna asking, who are you? Your line was a thousand suns. Today, the answer.

The New Mexico desert, before dawn. A bomb is tested, and a blinding light fills the sky. Years later, in a 1965 television documentary, J. Robert Oppenheimer, who led the scientists who built it, remembered what went through his mind. He had studied Sanskrit and read the Gita in the original. He recalled a line, in his own words: now I am become death, the destroyer of worlds. So what does the Sanskrit actually say?
screen: `THE NEW MEXICO DESERT.` → `A BLINDING LIGHT.` → `A LINE FROM THE GITA.`

segments.voice: Verse thirty-two begins: kalo 'smi. I am kala. Kala means time. It can also carry the sense of death, the way time eventually brings everything to an end, which is how Oppenheimer rendered it. The verse goes on: I am time, grown mighty, destroyer of worlds, here to bring the worlds to their end. Then the line that hits Arjuna hardest: even without you, none of these warriors lined up in the opposing ranks will survive. Back in chapter one, Arjuna broke down at the thought of killing his teachers and his great-uncle. Krishna's answer is that time has already claimed them. Verse thirty-three: so stand up, win glory. They've already been struck down by me. You be only the instrument. Nimitta-matram: merely the occasion, the tool. Verse thirty-four names them: Drona, Bhishma, Karna, and the rest, already slain. Don't be distressed. Fight. This is one of the hardest passages in the Gita, and readers have taken it in very different ways. Some read it as it stands: a warrior's duty in a just war, and the truth that no one controls who lives and who dies. Mahatma Gandhi read the whole battlefield as an allegory of the war inside each person, and took the Gita as a teaching of nonviolence. Either way, the verse sets two things side by side: time, which no one commands, and a part each person is asked to play without being in charge of the ending.

segments.voice: Listen for time: a clock ticking, your heartbeat, the breath coming and going, each one arriving and leaving, none of them staying. Then think of one thing you're trying to control the ending of, and just for this sit, set the ending down. Your part is the next breath, and the next.
Kala. Time, which brings everything to its end. Gita eleven, thirty-two: grown mighty, destroyer of worlds. Oppenheimer rendered it as death.

199.title: Arjuna's terror and praise (11.35–11.46)
199.hook: Arjuna realizes his best friend is God, and remembers every joke he ever made
199.howItsDone: Arjuna's hymn of praise in Gita 11.36–46 is recited by many Hindus in worship, and his plea for forgiveness shapes a common prayer habit of asking pardon for any disrespect shown in worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kala: I am Time, and be only the instrument. Your line was time. Today, Arjuna answers, trembling.

Your oldest friend, the one you've known forever. You've teased them, beaten them at cards, shared a bed on a camping trip, eaten off their plate without asking, called them ridiculous nicknames. Then one day you find out who they really are, and it's bigger than anything you ever imagined. Your first thought might not be wow. It might be: oh no. All those jokes. All those times I treated you like just anybody. That's exactly where Arjuna is in today's verses, trembling, palms pressed together.
screen: `YOUR OLDEST FRIEND.` → `THE TEASING, THE NICKNAMES.` → `OH NO. ALL THOSE JOKES.`

segments.voice: Sanjaya says Arjuna bows, trembling, and speaks with a choked voice. First, praise. It's right that the world rejoices in you and loves you. The frightened spirits flee in every direction, and the perfected ones bow. Why wouldn't they? You are the first god, the ancient person, the final resting place of the universe. You are the wind, death, fire, the lord of waters, the moon, the father of all creatures, and the great-grandfather. Then a line from someone who doesn't know where to put himself: bowing to you a thousand times, and again, and again. Bowing in front, bowing behind, bowing on every side. Then the confession, verses forty-one and forty-two. Thinking you were just my friend, I called you rashly: hey Krishna, hey Yadava, hey friend. I didn't know how great you were. Out of carelessness, or out of love, whatever disrespect I showed you as a joke, while playing, resting, sitting or eating, alone or in front of others, I ask you to forgive it, immeasurable one. Verse forty-four: bear with me as a father with a son, a friend with a friend, a lover with the beloved. Notice what he asks for. Not distance. Not a return to formality. He asks for the relationship to hold. And verse forty-five: I'm thrilled to have seen what no one has seen, and my mind is shaking with fear. Please, show me the form I know. Terror and praise, both at once.

segments.voice: Think of someone you've taken for granted, a parent, a partner, a friend who's always there, and see them the way Arjuna finally saw Krishna: bigger, more precious than you usually let yourself notice. Let a little awe come in. Then silently say what Arjuna said, forgive me for treating you like just anybody, and, like him, ask for the closeness to stay.
Sakha. Friend, companion, one of the careless names Arjuna regrets calling Krishna. Seeing his friend as God, he bows a thousand times, and asks forgiveness for every careless word.

200.title: The gentle form returns (11.47–11.55)
200.hook: after the thousand suns, the friend's face comes back, and Arjuna can breathe again
200.howItsDone: Much Hindu worship is directed to God in a gentle, familiar form, an image of Krishna, Rama, Shiva or the Goddess, and many devotees cite Gita 11.54–55 to say that loving devotion, not ritual alone, is how God is truly known.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sakha: Arjuna's terror and praise, and a friend asking to be forgiven for every joke. Your line was forgive my familiarity. Today is day two hundred, two hundred days on this path, and chapter eleven ends.

A child wakes from a nightmare, shaking in the dark. A parent comes in and turns on the small lamp by the bed. Same room. Same shadows in the corners. But now there's a familiar face, and a voice that says, it's okay, I'm here. The child can breathe again. Arjuna has seen the whole universe blazing in Krishna's body, mouths and fire and time itself. And he asked: please, show me the form I know.
screen: `A NIGHTMARE IN THE DARK.` → `A SMALL LAMP, A FAMILIAR FACE.` → `SHOW ME THE FORM I KNOW.`

segments.voice: Verse forty-seven: out of grace, through my own power, I showed you this highest form, full of light, universal, infinite, first. No one but you has seen it before. Verse forty-eight: not by the Vedas, not by sacrifice, not by study, not by gifts, not by rituals, not by fierce austerities can I be seen in this form by anyone but you. Then verse forty-nine, the tender turn. Don't be afraid. Don't be bewildered by this terrible form of mine. Let your fear go, be glad at heart, and see my familiar form again. Sanjaya tells what happens. Krishna shows his own form again, and, becoming gentle in form, saumya, the great soul comforts the frightened Arjuna. Saumya is a lovely word: gentle, mild, moon-like, cool after heat. Arjuna, verse fifty-one: seeing this gentle human form of yours, I'm myself again. I've come back to my nature. Then Krishna says what the whole chapter was pointing at. This form is very hard to see; even the gods long to see it. Not by Vedas, not by austerity, not by gifts or sacrifice. By devotion alone, bhakti, undivided, can I be known like this, seen truly, and entered. And the chapter's last verse, which some call the essence of the whole Gita: whoever works for me, holds me as the goal, is devoted to me, free of attachment, and without hatred toward any being, comes to me. Without hatred toward any being. After the thousand suns, the friend's face, and the way to it: by devotion alone.
screen: `NO ONE BUT YOU HAS SEEN IT.` · `DON'T BE AFRAID.` · `SAUMYA: GENTLE, MOON-LIKE.` · `WITHOUT HATRED TOWARD ANY BEING.` · then, large: `BY DEVOTION ALONE.`

segments.voice: Breathe out slowly, as if after a fright, and let your shoulders drop. Picture a familiar, gentle face, of God if you pray, or of someone who has comforted you, and let it say what Krishna said: don't be afraid. Stay with the gentleness, cool and quiet, like moonlight.
Saumya. Gentle, mild, moon-like: the form Krishna takes again after the vision, comforting the frightened Arjuna. He says he's truly seen by devotion alone.
Your line: by devotion alone. Saumya, gentle as moonlight after the heat. Two hundred days, and counting.

201.title: Form or formless? (12.1–12.7)
201.hook: love God with a face, or seek the reality beyond all faces? Arjuna asks which is better
201.howItsDone: Hindus worship God both with form (saguna), through images, names and stories, and as formless (nirguna), through silent meditation; many practice both, and chapter twelve is often read to honor each.

segments.voice: Yesterday, saumya: the gentle form returns, and God known by devotion alone. Your line was by devotion alone. Today, chapter twelve, the chapter of devotion.

In one Hindu home there's a shrine with a small image of Krishna, dressed in real clothes, offered food, put to bed at night. In another, someone sits in silence, eyes closed, and will tell you that God has no form at all, beyond every image and every name. Both are Hindu. And teachers have long disagreed about which comes closer. Arjuna has just seen God in an overwhelming cosmic form, then in a gentle human one. So chapter twelve opens with the obvious next question.
screen: `A SMALL IMAGE, DRESSED AND FED.` → `SILENCE, BEYOND EVERY FORM.` → `WHICH COMES CLOSER?`

segments.voice: Verse one, Arjuna: some are always devoted to you, worshiping you. Others worship the imperishable, the unmanifest. Which of these knows yoga best? Verse two, Krishna: those who fix their minds on me, always devoted, with the highest faith, I consider the most united. But then verses three and four: those who worship the imperishable, which can't be described, the unmanifest, present everywhere, beyond thought, unchanging, unmoving, firm, holding the senses in check, even-minded everywhere, delighting in the good of all beings, they also reach me. Both arrive. Verse five names the difference: the difficulty is greater for those whose minds are set on the unmanifest, because that path is hard for embodied beings. Beings with bodies love faces. And verses six and seven: those who offer all their actions to me, and meditate on me with undivided devotion, I quickly lift out of the ocean of death and rebirth. Hindu teachers have read this passage very differently. In Advaita Vedanta, following Shankara, the formless is the final truth, and the path of form is the gentler road for many people. In devotional schools, following teachers like Ramanuja, devotion to the personal Lord is itself the highest, and they read verse two that way. Both readings keep what the text says: both arrive, and one road is harder. Form or formless? Krishna's answer: either way.

segments.voice: For one minute, picture a face or an image that feels sacred to you, a deity, a teacher, a loved one, a candle flame, and hold it with warmth. For the next, let the image dissolve and rest in what's left: silence, space, awareness without a shape. Notice which feels closer today; there's no wrong answer, and the Gita says both arrive.

Avyakta, the unmanifest, what Krishna calls the formless beyond every image. Gita twelve: those devoted to God with a form, and those who seek the formless, both reach him; the formless path is harder for embodied beings.
Your line: either way. A face, or the silence, and either can be the road. Day two hundred one, done.

202.title: The ladder of practice (12.8–12.12)
202.hook: Krishna gives a path with a step for every kind of day
202.howItsDone: Many Hindus read Gita 12.8–12.12 as permission to begin wherever they are: some meditate, some keep a daily practice like japa, and many simply offer their ordinary work and let go of the result.

segments.voice: Yesterday, avyakta: form or formless, and Krishna's answer that both arrive. Your line was either way. Today, what to do when neither feels possible.

The first week after an injury, a good physical therapist says: today, walk to the door and back. You can't. Fine. Stand up and sit down five times. You can't do that either. Fine. Squeeze this ball. Nobody leaves the room with nothing to do; there's always a smaller step that still counts. Chapter twelve has a stretch that works exactly like that. Krishna has just named the goal. Then, instead of repeating it louder, he hands Arjuna smaller and smaller steps.
screen: `CAN'T WALK TO THE DOOR?` → `STAND UP AND SIT DOWN.` → `THERE'S ALWAYS A SMALLER STEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the ladder, verses eight through eleven, from the top. Fix your mind on me, let your understanding rest in me, and you will live in me. That's the whole goal in one sentence. Verse nine: if you can't hold your mind steady on me, seek me through practice. The Sanskrit is abhyasa, coming back again and again. It first came up in chapter six, with the restless mind. Verse ten: if you can't even practice, make your work for my sake. Do your ordinary actions as an offering, and you'll reach perfection that way. Verse eleven, the bottom rung: if you can't do even that, take refuge in me, keep yourself in check, and give up the fruit of all your actions. Just let go of how it turns out. Four rungs, and each one below the top begins the same way: if you can't. There's no scolding in it. No verse says you've failed. Each one says, then here's the next thing. Then verse twelve turns the ladder around. Knowledge is better than practice. Meditation is better than knowledge. And giving up the fruit of action is better than meditation, because peace follows that letting go right away. The lowest rung holds something the higher ones need. Commentators read this verse in different ways and don't rank the steps alike. What the text does is plain: it leaves no one without a step, however busy or scattered.

If even that feels like too much today, quietly dedicate one thing you'll do later, and if you can't manage that, simply let go of how today will turn out. Any rung counts.

203.title: The one dear to me (12.13–12.20)
203.hook: Krishna ends the chapter on devotion with a portrait, not a ritual
203.carry: free from hate, friendly to all
203.howItsDone: Gita chapter twelve, the chapter of bhakti, is short, and many Hindus memorize or recite it; its closing verses (12.13–12.20) are often read as a description of the devotee's character.

segments.voice: Yesterday, abhyasa: the ladder of practice. Fix your mind; if you can't, practice; if you can't, work as offering; if you can't, let go of the fruit. Your line was find the smaller rung.

There's a kind of friend who doesn't hold grudges. Who's the same at a wedding and a hospital. Who doesn't need anyone to agree with them. People leave their kitchen lighter than they came in, and nobody's quite sure how. Chapter twelve is the chapter of bhakti, devotion. You might expect it to end with instructions: which offering, which mantra, how many times. It doesn't. It ends with a portrait of a person. Eight verses, and a refrain that keeps coming back.
screen: `THE FRIEND WHO HOLDS NO GRUDGES.` → `NOT A RITUAL.` → `A PORTRAIT.`

segments.voice: Verse thirteen opens the portrait. The one who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free of mine and free of ego, the same in pleasure and pain, forgiving. The Sanskrit starts adveshta sarva-bhutanam: without hatred toward all beings. Then maitra, friendly, and karuna, compassion. Again and again the verses close with some version of the same small phrase: sa me priyah. That one is dear to me. It's Krishna's voice, and it's tender. Verse fifteen turns it both ways: the world does not shrink from them, and they do not shrink from the world. Nobody is afraid of them, and they aren't afraid of anybody. The portrait keeps going. Not elated, not hating, not grieving, not craving. The same to friend and enemy, in honor and insult, in cold and heat. Quiet. Content with whatever comes. And a surprising word in verse nineteen: aniketa, without a fixed home. Commentators read it as someone who doesn't cling to their house as the center of the universe, not necessarily someone homeless. Notice what isn't on the list. No rank. No caste. No particular ritual. The chapter on devotion ends by describing how a devoted person treats everyone else. Verse twenty closes it: those who follow this with faith are exceedingly dear. That closes the chapter, and the week. It started with the vision that shook Arjuna, and it ends with a kind face.
screen: `HATING NO BEING.` · `NO ONE AFRAID OF THEM.` · `THE SAME IN HONOR AND INSULT.` · `THAT ONE IS DEAR TO ME.` · then, large: `THE ONE DEAR TO ME.`

segments.voice: Recall one recent moment of praise and one of criticism, a compliment and a sharp word, and hold each for a breath, noticing what happens in you. Then, for a few breaths, let both sit side by side: the same in honor and insult, as verse eighteen puts it. You don't have to feel nothing; just stay even.
Priya, dear, beloved. Gita twelve, thirteen to twenty: a portrait of the devoted person, free of hate, friendly and kind, and the refrain, sa me priyah, that one is dear to me.
Your line: free from hate, friendly to all. The vision in chapter eleven, form or formless, the ladder, the portrait: that's the week.

what it means: in Gita 12 devotion ends in character: free of hate, friendly, the same in praise and insult.
what a scholar hears: 12.13 opens 'adveshta sarva-bhutanam maitrah karuna eva ca'; the refrain 'sa me priyah' recurs through 12.20.
